item.title: 🔴 Understand the agentic supply chain: 5 things CIOs must know
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Software supply chain risk used to have a fairly contained definition: open-source packages, build pipelines, and the occasional compromised maintainer account. AI agents have changed that. An agent assembles capability at runtime, pulling in models, MCP servers, libraries, code, tools, skills, and plugins, then acts on its findings. Agents operate at machine speed in parallelized workflows at speed and volume far greater than those of human-paced developers.

This differs from the dependencies CIOs have long governed. An agent’s tool catalog can change the day after approval, and the agent will trust whatever shows up the next time it looks. OWASP now includes Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04) in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications, describing risks that “arise when agents, tools, and related artifacts they work with are provided by third parties and may be malicious, compromised, or tampered with in transit.”

item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

To succeed today, CIOs must be strategic partners. It’s no longer something to work toward achieving.

“What used to be an aspiration, having a seat at the table, that’s now needed,” says George Westerman, a senior lecturer at the MIT Sloan School of Management, founder of the Global Opportunity Forum, and co-chair of the MIT Sloan CIO Leadership Award. “AI has made it more important for the CIO to be able to exercise influence and give advice, because now you have a major technology that every C-suite person is wondering about and feels they need to use, and, given its transformative nature throughout the organization, this is where the skills of a CIO who is a strategic partner can be really useful.”

That, though, may not be enough for CIOs in the future.

The CIOs of tomorrow will be crafting the vision of what is possible for the organization, advising their C-suite colleagues on integrating agents into their teams, and navigating high-pressure situations, says Westerman and other IT leaders.

item.title: 🔵 The technology maturity paradox: Why more capabilities can make IT harder
item.description:

Technology maturity is generally considered a sign of progress. Organizations modernize their infrastructure and capabilities, introduce advanced analytics, and invest in AI, all with the expectation that these improvements will make the business more capable, efficient, and competitive.

But there’s a paradox emerging in enterprise IT: The more sophisticated an organization’s technology environment becomes, the more difficult it can be to manage. Every new capability may expand what the business can accomplish while also increasing the number of dependencies, decisions, and stakeholders that must be coordinated. At this rate, technological progress can outpace the organization’s ability to manage it.

item.title: 🔵 Why technology is no longer IT’s scarcest resource
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential budget or licensing impact — verify renewal terms and forecast changes.

For much of the history of enterprise IT, technology itself was a limiting factor. Organizations had to make difficult choices about which systems they could afford and which capabilities were realistic to deploy. Technology leaders built their strategies around those constraints.

Today, the challenge looks different. Cloud platforms, advanced analytics, automation, and AI have made sophisticated capabilities accessible to organizations of nearly every size. Microsoft’s expanding portfolio, from Azure and Fabric to Power Platform and Copilot, illustrates just how quickly the range of available options has grown. But greater access to technology has made the job of the tech leader more complicated.

The scarcest resources in IT today are the attention, organizational context, and judgment required to distinguish meaningful opportunities from distractions. The CIO’s challenge is no longer simply understanding what technology can do, but determining what deserves the organization’s finite capacity to act.

OpenAI maintains an official GitHub repository of skills that teach AI agents how to work with various platforms and services. As an official skill, these components are often given an implicit level of trust because they are contributed or vetted by verified vendors.

item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

The Linux kernel’s networking stack was found vulnerable to a guest-to-host escape attack, in which an attacker operating inside a virtual machine (VM) could cross the isolation boundary and access the underlying host.

Dubbed PwnEscape and tracked as CVE-2026-99999, a flaw allowed guest-controlled packet metadata to trigger a write that changes an IPv4 header after the kernel has already processed it. That flaw could be chained with additional exploitation techniques to achieve host-level code execution.

The problem was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of Pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, announced on August 18. The challenge invited researchers to test the isolation boundaries of Vercel’s sandboxing infrastructure, including whether they could escape the virtual machine itself and reach the host.

Companies routinely rely on authenticating the identities of humans who access sensitive company data across their networks. There’s an established and accepted set of protocols, done upfront and in a zero-trust approach – either we know who you are and let you in, or you’re locked out. The same framework needs to be applied to AI agents, posthaste.

Companies are increasingly using AI agents developed in-house, or by their vendors, partners, or clients, or, unfortunately, criminals. This can quickly add up to thousands of agents across their infrastructure and supply chains. Non-human identities outnumber human ones 45 to 1 on average in the enterprise and 144 to 1 in cloud-native environments, an increase of 44% in one year, per a recent report.

item.title: 🔴 No click required: How the ad industry became a pipeline for mercenary spyware
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

That ad you just scrolled past on your phone but barely spared a look or click? It could be tracking your movements and collecting your data, without you having to do a thing.

This “zero-click mercenary spyware,” dubbed “AdFection,” is increasingly exploiting a sprawling online advertising ecosystem ripe for abuse, according to researchers at The Citizen Lab. One top actor in the space, Discover-Tech, runs the Controlium platform that allows cyber criminals to “precisely profile and de-anonymize” millions of users, fingerprint them, and automatically infect their devices when an ad is displayed.

Troublingly, Discover-Tech is successfully masquerading as a legitimate ad company across the online ad sales environment, the researchers said, listed as a “certified” and “approved” vendor by the likes of Google and IAB Europe.

item.title: 🔵 Secure your AI estate: 5 things CIOs must know about AI agents
item.description:
Why this matters: Potential data exposure — review monitoring and incident-response readiness.

What CIOs need to know about AI agents

Enterprise AI adoption is entering a new phase. Generative AI gave employees new ways to create content and access information, primarily through AI web applications. Embedded AI copilots began helping them work natively in existing applications.

Now, AI agents are running locally on employee workstations, with expansive user permissions, and are increasingly capable of autonomously executing work.

An AI agent is an LLM-powered software system that can reason over context, make decisions, and pursue an objective with a degree of autonomy. Unlike conventional software built around predefined logic, agents introduce probabilistic, context-sensitive reasoning into how tasks are interpreted and executed. They can interpret changing inputs, determine what to do next, use tools and enterprise systems, and adapt as a task unfolds.

item.title: 🔵 What a cockatoo can teach us about the evidence AI wasn’t built to hear
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

AI systems do not make decisions from reality. They make decisions from representations of reality: records, observations, measurements, histories, labels, documents, and whatever else an organization has decided belongs in the data. That distinction sounds almost too obvious to be interesting, yet it becomes surprisingly easy to forget once an AI system can process thousands of records, identify patterns no person would notice, and return an answer that appears comprehensive. The sophistication of the analysis can distract us from a more basic problem: important information may never enter the decision process in a form the system can use.

Much of the responsible-AI conversation begins after that problem has already occurred. We ask whether a model is accurate, whether its recommendation can be explained, whether a human remains involved, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Those are necessary questions, but they assume that the relevant evidence made it into the decision somewhere. For the past half century or more, the teams running enterprise software stacks have nurtured a vast ecosystem of tools to keep software humming along. They’ve built CI/CD pipelines, elaborate test suites, code repositories, and tools galore, all with the goal of keeping the systems up and running.

Now AI is throwing a wrench into the whole endeavor. Software is now more complex and sometimes mysteriously unpredictable. Expectations are sky high, but no one is certain what to expect in good conscience.

Luckily, dozens of companies are rushing to build new tools designed to keep agentic stacks on the straight and narrow, delivering value to everyone. The field is rapidly evolving, probably having changed since you started reading this article.

Some of the tools involved in the emerging agent stack aren’t that different from what enterprise teams already have in store. In the end, LLMs are just piles of bits that need to be loaded into a processing chip, just like old-fashioned software. item.title: 🟠 Unplug your smart fridges, French supermarkets warned after cyberattack
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

More internet-connected refrigerators have joined the official list of those affected by a cyberattack that ruined stocks of chilled food at hundreds of French supermarkets over the weekend.

The French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) advised supermarkets to disconnect any refrigeration control systems with a public IP address from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, it suggested, they could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution, CERT-FR said.

CERT-FR’s initial warning on Monday listed only Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series refrigeration controllers as affected, advising supermarkets to update the firmware of their systems, set the security level to “strict,” and ensure that default passwords had been changed.
